newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Nordics push for lower EU sulphur-in-fuel norms.
newsitem.headline: Nordics push for lower EU sulphur-in-fuel norms.

text.p: Sweden and Finland have asked their EU partners to back stricter norms on sulphur content in diesel and petrol after a study they sponsored said introduction costs would not be as high as previously thought.

Swedish environment minister Anna Lindh and Finnish counterpart Pekka Haavisto sent details of a study by consultants Arthur D Little to fellow environment ministers ahead of their two-day Brussels meeting starting on March 3.

Study findings, released to reporters, put the capital investment cost of cutting sulphur content in road transport gasoline to 30 parts per million (ppm) at 2.94 billion European currency units, 17 percent less than estimated by the European Commission's own research findings.
Cutting sulphur content in diesel to 50 ppm would cost 5.99 billion or 55 percent less than the Commission figure, it said.

Lindh and Haavisto told ministers that existing draft proposals on sulphur content, setting average market-value targets for the year 2000 at 150 ppm for petrol and 300 ppm for diesel, would inhibit the introduction of direct-injection engines and their potential for fuel savings.

They said existing plans would also delay the introduction of catalysts intended to cut nitrous oxide emissions, which are among the main precursor gases causing the formation of ground-level ozone, and would be two to three times less effective in curbing fine soot emissions from diesel vehicles.

The Nordics' intervention, citing a study produced by the same consultants used by the Commission in its original proposal, comes after Euro-MPs announced their intentions to tighten significantly the Commission's proposals of last June.

The original draft rules, contained in the EU's so-called auto-oil programme, set out a series of quality standards for fuel and engine emission standards required by the year 2000. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
